models.headline: Qwen 3.8 27B on a laptop reads raw model weights and guesses the game they were trained on
models.summary: Simon Willison ran a paper's test on Qwen 3.8 27B locally and it guessed Pong and Breakout, though it missed Freeway.
models.why_it_matters: You can run this kind of test on your own laptop with LM Studio and the llm tool, but it took close to an hour per answer.

extra.candidate_title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
extra.source_text: Simon Willison’s Weblog Newsletter Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too 3rd November 2026 Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: breakout/prompt.txt freeway/prompt.txt pacman/prompt.txt pong/prompt.txt I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \ -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \ llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \ -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here’s the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. Confidence: 72% This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. Description: The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. Confidence: 75% And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Confidence: 88% Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s that transcript —Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”. The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample: What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right? That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort. It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways. models.headline: Astra reads and edits neural network weights, not just text
models.summary: The most surprising result: a frontier LLM named Astra fixed a small math model's reasoning loops by editing 0.016% of its weights.

extra.candidate_title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
extra.source_text: 日本語 Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights Authors Rikiya Takehi * Jayden Teoh * Alex Zhang Omar Khattab Affiliations MIT CSAIL MIT CSAIL MIT CSAIL MIT CSAIL Published November 2, 2026 TL;DR We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights , using a variety of recent tools and algorithms or even via direct weight editing. These results show sparks of Weight-Space Programming, which may extend beyond what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability. Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights . Read Which game was this neural network trained on? Astra reads the 17,253 weights, with no tools Breakout 99% confident Fix A trained policy never gets the car over the strip. Astra edits 3.5% of the weights, in one shot 100% success, up from 0% Improve Make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math. 7.9% base 7.9% Astra’s edit Astra edits the weights in a Python kernel, with no training 48.1% on MATH-500, up from 7.9% If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible. Today, weights are written by optimization , by custom networks trained to write them , or by compilers from formal programs . In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals. Weight-Space Programming For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models . We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks . After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms. In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks . In Weight-Space Programming , a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all. In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch . We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models: LLMs can read neural network weights: In Experiments 1 to 3, we ask Astra questions like what game a network was trained to play, what shape is drawn by a diffusion model, and which language a small language model was trained on. In Experiment 7, we ask which of two language models was trained to be sycophantic. LLMs can fix neural network weights: In Experiment 4, we ask Astra to fix a network that’s failing at some physical control task. In Experiment 8, we ask it to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math, and its fix improves instruction following too. LLMs can write neural network weights from scratch: In Experiment 5, we ask Astra for networks that play three MinAtar games, and in Experiment 6, for a network that plays Go. Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers. In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights. Experiment 1 Can Astra tell which game the network was trained on just from the weights? We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read. For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from. Setup Games: our own grid versions of Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man and Freeway, all on the same 10×10 grid with the same five actions Network: MLP 500 → 32 → 32 → 5, tanh (17,253 weights), the same for every game Input: the 10×10 grid in 5 channels: agent, moving objects, reward targets, obstacles, previous frame Output: 5 action logits: no-op, up, down, left, right Training: PPO, 1 billion steps, the same settings for every game, the best of 3 seeds per game Astra gets: all the weights as text, and the grid and actions described without any game named It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart. Experiment 2 Can Astra tell what the diffusion model will generate? Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models. We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes. Setup Models: three diffusion models (DDPM) of 12×12 grayscale images, one each for filled circles, squares and triangles Network: MLP 160 → 64 → 64 → 144, ReLU (23,824 weights) Input: a noisy image (144 pixels) and the diffusion step (16 numbers) Output: the clean image (144 pixels) Training: Adam, 40,000 steps, batch 512 Astra gets: all the weights as text, with no shape named, and is told not to compute any forward pass Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights. Experiment 3 Can Astra tell what a language model learned, from the middle of the network alone? Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers. We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python code The Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub . , Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input. We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does . Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one. Trained on Astra’s answer (& confidence), two attempts Copying heads Astra names (layer.head) Copying heads, ground truth Python Python (0.56), Python (0.52) 2.1, 3.1, 3.5 2.1, 3.1, 3.5 Romaji romaji (0.55), romaji (0.62) 3.3 3.3 English English (0.58), English (0.48) 3.1 3.1 Where the copying heads are … tot al … tot al A copying head finds the same letters earlier in the text and copies what came after them. copying head other head Rows are layers 0 to 3, columns are heads 0 to 5 Astra: from the weights. Measured: by running the model Python Astra Measured Romaji Astra Measured English Astra Measured Figure 1: The copying heads Astra read from the weights match the measured ones in all three models. Setup Models: character-level transformers, 4 layers × 6 heads, width 384 (7.16 million weights), 28 characters: a–z, space and newline Training: 1 billion characters each, of Python code, Japanese literature in romaji (Aozora Bunko), or English Wikipedia Astra gets: the weights of the four transformer blocks only, with no input layer, no output layer and no labels on the 384 dimensions, and Python to analyze them, up to 100 runs Not allowed: running the network or any of its layers on any input, real, random or made up, and search. We checked every run Asked: which of the three texts the network was trained on, and what each head does Truth: each head measured by running the network on a random string repeated twice. Copying heads score 0.22 to 0.55, every other head at most 0.02. Astra never sees this The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to tot al when tot al came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along ( Figure 1 ). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al. , which we never mentioned to Astra. Code repeats names far more than prose, so many copying heads pointed to Python. Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. extra.source_text: DeepSeek Harness: Everything is a Plugin. # DeepSeek Harness English | [中文](README.zh.md) DeepSeek Harness (`dsh`) is an open-source agent harness developed by [DeepSeek AI](https://deepseek.com). It is built on an **everything-is-a-plugin** architecture and powered by [Cordis](https://github.com/cordiverse/cordis), whose design is described in [_A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25512). Documentation: [https://deepseek-harness.github.io/deepseek-harness/](https://deepseek-harness.github.io/deepseek-harness/) ## Developer preview DeepSeek Harness is in _developer preview_ and iterating rapidly. **THERE WILL BE COMPATIBILITY-BREAKING CHANGES.** Review the [safety notice](SAFETY.md) before running the project. ## Run ### Run from `npm` Install `Node.js`, then run: ```sh npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web ``` The command starts the Web UI at `http://127.0.0.1:3080` by default and opens it in the default browser for a local launch. An SSH launch only prints the host URL because the SSH client or editor owns the local forwarded address. Pass `--no-open` to run the server without opening a browser. See [Web UI guide](docs/user/guide/index.md). ### Run from source To run from a repository checkout: ```sh git clone https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness.git cd deepseek-harness pnpm install pnpm run build pnpm dsh web ``` `pnpm run build` prepares the repository artifacts. `pnpm dsh web` uses those built artifacts without rebuilding. ## Community and support - Submit feedback or bug reports through [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/discussions). - Add the [`dsh-plugin`](https://github.com/topics/dsh-plugin) topic to your plugin repository for discoverability. - Join DeepSeek Harness Discord community. ## Contributing See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). ## Development Start with the [development guide](docs/development.md) and [architecture documentation](docs/architecture.md). `pnpm run dev:web` builds, serves, and rebuilds client bundles on source edits in one terminal, and `make help` lists the matching Make targets for Web and Desktop; the guide's application commands section owns the full table. For agents, follow [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). ## Citation ```bibtex @misc{deepseek-harness2026, title={DeepSeek Harness: Everything is a Plugin}, author={DeepSeek-AI}, year={2026}, publisher={GitHub}, howpublished={\url{https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness}}, } ``` ## License [MIT](LICENSE) Third-party dependencies and their licenses are disclosed in [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

extra.description: 让你的命令行 Agent 在后台自己接活、自己跟进到底；平时不烦你，遇到拿不准的事才发卡片找你拍板。
extra.source_text:
让你的命令行 Agent 在后台自己接活、自己跟进到底；平时不烦你，遇到拿不准的事才发卡片找你拍板。 # Agent Autoloop **让你的命令行 Agent 在后台自己接活、自己跟进到底；平时不烦你，遇到拿不准的事才发卡片找你拍板。** **中文** | [English](README.en.md) [上手](#上手) · [场景模板](#拿来即用的场景模板) · [插件](#插件体系四个方向都能自由替换) · [内核](#内核的四个机制) · [文档](#更多文档) ![架构图](docs/architecture.svg) ## 它解决什么问题？ 平时我们用 Claude Code、Codex 这类命令行 Agent，大多是“人守着终端用”：你输一句话，盯着它跑，等它问你下一步；一旦关掉窗口或者人走开，事情就断了。 **Agent Autoloop** 是一个极轻量的自动化中台。它把任务调度做成一个零外部依赖的**内核**，把事件来源、Agent、通知通道，甚至代码上线流水线全部拆成可随时插拔的**插件**。 - **一台电脑、一条命令就能跑。** 装在你的 Windows、Mac 或 Linux 上，不用买云服务器，也不用开放公网端口。 - **一行配置接新 Agent。** 不需要 SDK，也不需要改 Agent 源码，能接收提示词并打印最后一条回复的命令行工具都能接。 - **没有后台界面。** 需要你拍板时把卡片推到飞书、钉钉、企微、Slack、Discord 或桌面通知；想看全局进展，敲一行命令。 ## 上手 支持 Windows、macOS 和 Linux。需要 Node 24 或更新、Git，以及一个已经登录的命令行 Agent；macOS/Linux 还需要 curl，不需要 GitHub 账号。也可以把[安装说明](INSTALL.md)交给你的 Agent。 Windows PowerShell： ```powershell irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/KKKKhazix/agent-autoloop/main/install.ps1 | iex ``` macOS / Linux： ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/KKKKhazix/agent-autoloop/main/install.sh | sh ``` 安装和 `agent-autoloop update` 都装最新的 [Release](https://github.com/KKKKhazix/agent-autoloop/releases)，那是通过了全部检查的版本。 装好后用你本机的 Agent 真实走一遍“提问 → 退出等回复 → 拍板 → 接着干完”： ```bash agent-autoloop try ``` 下面是在终端里的真实输出： ```text 事件发出去了，Agent 开始干活…… Agent 结束了这一轮，问了你一个问题。它现在不占进程、不花 Token。 【等你决定】#1 试跑：选一个颜色 这是一次试跑，选哪个都行。 1. 蓝色 2. 绿色 回答：agent-autoloop answer 1 <序号> 答完运行 agent-autoloop status，能看到它接着把活干完。 ``` 交互终端里直接输入数字回车；非交互终端运行 `agent-autoloop answer 1 2` 选择“绿色”。再跑 `agent-autoloop status`，就能看到它接上刚才的会话并显示“你选了绿色，试跑通过”，还有今天和最近 7 天的轮数、Token 和费用（[统计口径](skills/agent-autoloop/SKILL.md#看情况回答)）。 ## 一件事怎么转起来 编号和上面的架构图一一对应： 1. **新事件进来。** 早上 9 点的定时任务、GitHub 上新提的 Issue、业务系统报的错，都变成一条标准事件送进内核。 2. **按规则派活。** 内核照你写的规则，决定交给哪个 Agent、去哪个目录干。同一件事排队时又来的消息，会合并成一轮处理。 3. **干完一轮就退出。** Agent 把结果写在最后一条回复里，进程直接退出。 4. **拿不准才问你。** 碰到删数据、重启服务、花钱、对外发消息这类事，内核通过飞书或桌面通知发一张卡片给你。等你回复期间，它不占后台进程，也不消耗 Token。 5. **点一下，接着干。** 你选完，它接上原来的对话，把剩下的活干完。 能自己搞定的事走图上方的自动闭环：直接办完，或者约个时间（比如半小时后）再醒来复查，全程不打扰你。 ## 日常怎么配？ ### 写一份规则（`rules.json`） 不需要写胶水代码。打开 `~/.agent-autoloop/rules.json`，在 `rules` 里写清楚**什么事、交给谁、在哪个目录干**。`to` 填 `agents` 里已有的名字。比如每天早上 9 点写早报： ```json { "name": "早报", "when": { "cron": "0 9 * * *" }, "to": "codex", "cwd": "~/notes", "prompt": "整理昨天的笔记和提交，写今天的早报。" } ``` 外部事件写法一样，只是要先接好来源。比如有人提新 Issue 时交给 Codex，先按[说明](skills/agent-autoloop/SKILL.md#接一个事件插件)在 `sources` 里登记 `github`： ```json { "name": "处理 issue", "when": { "source": "github", "types": ["issues.opened"] }, "to": "codex", "cwd": "~/code/app", "skill": "handle-issue", "parallel": 3 } ``` `agent-autoloop pause <规则>`、`resume <规则>` 暂停和恢复一条规则，暂停期间到点不跑、来事件不接，恢复后不补跑；`agent-autoloop run <规则>` 立即跑一轮。这些记在中台的日志里，不改 `rules.json`。 保存后几秒内自动生效，可以运行 `agent-autoloop check` 检查，`agent-autoloop check <文件>` 检查一份草稿，不碰正在跑的中台；`agent-autoloop rules explain` 看生效的规则和下次定时，`agent-autoloop emit <类型> --dry-run` 预演一条事件会派给谁（不连接中台、不写日志）。就算改错了，或者文件被删、读不到，系统也会继续按旧规则跑，并发卡片提醒你。 ### Agent 怎么跟中台配合？ 中台对 Agent 只有一个约定：**在最后一条回复里交代结果**。事情办完了，正常输出一句结论就行。需要向你请示时，在回复末尾附一段 `agent-autoloop` 代码块： ````text 订单已经核对完毕，库存充足。 ```agent-autoloop { "ask": [{ "title": "怎么发货？", "text": "两种方式今天都能发出。", "options": ["快递", "自提"], "key": "shipping" }] } ``` ```` 除了提问（`ask`），还能发通知（`notice`）、关闭已解决的卡片（`resolve`）、预约复查（`later`）和触发新事件（`events`）。通告不需要回答，但结案时可以顺手写一句处理说明，这句话会留在卡片上；只是告诉一声的通告标成 `fyi`，不带按钮。万一 JSON 写错了，中台只让它在原会话里重写最后这段回复，不会把已经干完的业务重做一遍；重写也失败时，保留原结论并通知你回执没有生效（通用命令没有会话，直接走这一步）。接着旧会话跑也一样：会话接不上才开新的；接上了、干到一半断了，就算没跑成，过几分钟回到原会话重试，不开新会话重做。同一事项的新事件默认开新会话；规则写 `"resume": true` 就接着上一轮的会话。 ## 拿来即用的场景模板 每套模板都带规则、任务 Skill 和启用说明。 | 想做什么 | 已经封装好的流程 | |---|---| | [每日早报](examples/recipes/morning-brief/README.md) | 默认每天 8 点整理本地笔记和 Git 提交，写入 `briefs/YYYY-MM-DD.md` | | [跟进 GitHub Issue](examples/recipes/github-issues/README.md) | 每 5 分钟查新 Issue，在本地改代码并通知你查看；不提交、不推送、不回复 Issue | | [线上告警排查](examples/recipes/ops-alerts/README.md) | 接收报错、对照代码查原因，需要重启时发卡片询问，回答后继续 | | [用户反馈处理](examples/recipes/feedback/README.md) | 重读反馈当前状态、修复、交付核实、准备回复；需要决定时飞书问你，回答后继续 | | [网站巡检](examples/recipes/website-watch/README.md) | 每 5 分钟检查状态和关键内容，首次异常交给 Agent，持续异常不重复通知，恢复后更新原卡片 | | [飞书周报与业务摘要](examples/recipes/feishu-brief/README.md) | 周日 18 点按你的权限读汇报和指定表格，生成本地摘要；飞书只发简短摘要，完整稿留在本机 | | [收件箱分诊](examples/recipes/inbox-triage/README.md) | 默认每天 8 点读过去 24 小时的未读邮件，写成清单和回复草稿；不发送、不改邮箱状态 | | [PR 自动交付](skills/agent-autoloop/SKILL.md#交付流水线) | 打上 `deliver` 标签后，审查、等 CI、合并、等发布并核对线上版本 | **启用：** 打开对应说明，把任务 Skill 放进所用 Agent 的 skills 目录，把示例规则合入 `~/.agent-autoloop/rules.json`，替换电脑名和路径，再运行 `agent-autoloop check`。 反馈处理、网站巡检、飞书摘要和收件箱分诊默认使用北京时间，只发给本人的飞书私聊。样例数据都是虚构的；脚本和回执只用本地 HTTP 与假飞书 CLI 验证过，没有在真实账号上跑过完整业务。 更多模板：[Claude 委托 Codex 处理网页](examples/recipes/browser-handoff/README.md)、[每周代码清理](examples/skills/weekly-sweep/SKILL.md)、[交付 PR](examples/skills/ship-pr/SKILL.md)。 ## 插件体系：四个方向都能自由替换 内置插件随程序安装，填好配置即可启用；第三方插件用 `agent-autoloop add ` 安装。 | 方向 | 内置 | 配置 | |---|---|---| | **事件**：怎么发现新活 | [GitHub Webhook](plugins/github/source.ts)、[GitLab Webhook](plugins/gitlab/source.ts)、[HTTP 接口](docs/protocol.md#来源把世界变成事件)、[定时规则](skills/agent-autoloop/SKILL.md#改规则)、[Issue 轮询脚本](examples/watch-github-issues.sh) | [说明](skills/agent-autoloop/SKILL.md#接一个事件插件) | | **Agent**：谁来干活 | [Claude Code](plugins/claude/agent.ts)、[Codex](plugins/codex/agent.ts)、[ACP](plugins/acp/agent.ts)、[DeepSeek Harness](plugins/dsh/agent.ts)、[通用命令](plugins/command/agent.ts) | [说明](skills/agent-autoloop/SKILL.md#接一个-agent) | | **通道**：去哪找你拍板 | [桌面通知](plugins/desktop/channel.ts)（默认开启）、[飞书](plugins/feishu/channel.ts)、[钉钉 / 企微 / Slack / Discord](plugins/webhook/templates.ts) | [说明](skills/agent-autoloop/SKILL.md#接一个通道) | | **交付**：把 CI/CD 也做成插件 | [`delivery`](plugins/delivery/delivery.ts) | [说明](skills/agent-autoloop/SKILL.md#交付流水线) | **实测情况：** Claude Code、Codex 和 ACP（官方 Codex ACP 适配器）跑通了多轮问答和跨进程会话续接；飞书跑通了发送、按钮回调和卡片更新；四种 Webhook 模板只在本地模拟服务上验证过，GitLab Webhook 按官方文档的格式测试，没连过真实 GitLab。这些文字通道靠回答链接拍板，要把 `hub.publicUrl` 配成手机或电脑能打开的地址。 **内置 Agent 走第三方网关。** Claude Code、Codex 要接第三方模型服务，或者启动前要先设好环境变量，写一个设好变量再启动它的小脚本，在 Agent 里写 `"program": "脚本路径"`，会话续接和用量统计照旧，见[说明](skills/agent-autoloop/SKILL.md#接一个-agent)。 **其他命令行 Agent 一行接入。** 设置 `use: "command"` 并传入命令数组，`{prompt}` 作为独立参数传递，不会被当成 shell 代码执行。下面的命令整理自各家官方文档，我们还没有逐个跑过： | Agent | 接入命令 | |---|---| | [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/blob/master/docs/cli-help.md#dsh-headless) 旧版（内置插件要 0.2.2 或更新） | `dsh --profile headless {prompt}` | | [pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/cli.md) | `pi --print {prompt}` | | [OpenClaw](https://docs.openclaw.ai/cli/agent) | `openclaw agent exec {prompt}` | | [Hermes](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/cli) | `hermes chat -Q -q {prompt}` | | [Cursor](https://cursor.com/docs/cli/reference/parameters) | `agent -p --trust {prompt}` | | [WorkBuddy / CodeBuddy](https://www.codebuddy.ai/docs/cli/headless) | `codebuddy -p {prompt}` | 会说 ACP 的 Agent 用 `use: "acp"` 接，还能接着原来的会话做：[Gemini CLI](https://geminicli.com/docs/cli/acp-mode/) 写 `"command": ["gemini", "--acp"]`，[OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/docs/acp) 写 `"command": ["opencode", "acp"]`。这两条已经跑通了 ACP 握手（Gemini CLI 0.67.0、OpenCode 1.1.2），多轮问答和会话续接还没跑过。 **交付流水线。** 给 GitHub PR 打上 `deliver` 标签后，它会自己跟进到上线：**审代码 → 等 CI → 合并 PR → 等部署 → 核对线上版本**。审查和交付配置只从 `main` 读取，绝不在接单电脑上检出或运行 PR 里的代码；排队、并发和重试直接复用内核。 **写自己的插件。** 从 [Agent](examples/plugins/hello-agent/agent.ts)、[通道](examples/plugins/hello-channel/channel.ts)、[事件](examples/plugins/hello-source/source.ts) 三个可运行的最小模板开始，见[插件开发说明](docs/plugins.md)。要让 Agent 操作网页，先看[浏览器接入](docs/plugins.md#浏览器接入)。命令行和 [MCP](skills/agent-autoloop/SKILL.md#mcp-与密钥撤销) 也能查看和回答卡片。 ## 内核的四个机制 内核约 1850 行代码、零运行时依赖。它不读系统时钟、不用随机数、不向外发请求，插件主动连进来，账号凭据留在各自的插件里；同样的输入永远得出同样的结果。它把四个计算机领域的成熟做法用到了命令行 Agent 上： - **挂起零消耗**：等你拍板时进程直接退出，等待状态存在数据库里，Agent 不用一直挂着。你三天没回，这三天就没有 Agent 进程在跑、不花 Token，只有很轻的中台在后台等着；你一回答，它接着原来的对话继续干。 - **事件溯源**：所有状态都从一条只追加的日志算出来，日志和索引在同一个事务里写进磁盘，写完才应答。进程被强杀，已经确认的事不丢（整机断电没有单独测过）；任何一轮为什么跑、结果是什么，一条命令就能查清；数据格式变了就从日志重建，不用写迁移脚本。 - **指令数据分离**：思路和 SQL 参数化一样。Issue 的标题和正文等外部文字只作为资料放进文件，不拼进提示词，提示词里只有校验过字符的类型、编号和链接；用哪个 Agent、在哪个目录、什么权限，只由你本机的规则决定，事件里带 `cwd`、`agent`、`access` 字段会被直接拒收。 - **跳数熔断**：思路和网络包的 TTL 一样。Agent 交回的事件会再派给 Agent，层数一路累加，经过人工提问和定时复查也不清零，Agent 自己改不了；超过 8 层就只记录、不再派活，并发一张卡片告诉你。 ### 自己跑一遍 Windows 用 `npm run test:windows` 和 `node scripts/install-smoke-windows.ts`，运行共用行为测试与原生进程、安装检查；Unix shell 测试仍在 Linux/macOS 上跑。 在程序目录 `~/.agent-autoloop/app` 下运行： | 验证什么 | 命令 | |---|---| | 任何一轮的来龙去脉 | `agent-autoloop why 1` | | 20 万步模拟断网、丢包、崩溃和重复提交，一个种子就能复现 | `node sim/random.ts 24301 200000` | | 强杀进程 1000 次，已确认的记录一条不丢 | `node sim/crash.ts 1000 12648430` | | 下面的性能数字 | `npm run benchmark` | ```text 第 1 轮 · 演示 11-03 20:47:25 规则版本 #1 11-03 20:47:25 触发事件：来源 local · 类型 demo.start · 对象 example 11-03 20:47:25 local 领取（演示程序） 11-03 20:47:25 结束：演示完成 ``` ### 实测性能 Apple M5 Pro、24 GB、Node 24.21.0。写入逐条提交，事务落盘后才应答。 | 指标 | 实测 | |---|---:| | 冷启动 | 88.78 ms | | 空闲内存 | 59.94 MB RSS | | 1000 个同时等待的长轮询 | 170.49 MB RSS | | 持久化写入 | 2394 条/秒 | | 派活 p99 | 1.82 ms | | 排队 5000 时被挡下的心跳 p99 | 1.66 ms | | 110 万条事实时的启动 | 99.8 ms | | 内核行数（含空行和注释） | 约 1850 | | 运行时依赖 | 0 | 历史变大后，状态汇总会变慢，日志和索引也继续占磁盘；格式变化后的首次启动要从日志全量重建，110 万条用时 43.1 秒。[完整数据和测法](docs/protocol.md#历史增长实测)。 ## 用量与合规说明 中台直接调用你本机已经安装并登录好的命令行工具，不会读取或转存你的账号凭据。模型调用消耗算在你自己的账号名下，额度和使用范围遵循各家模型厂商的服务条款。 在高频自动化场景下，各家厂商通常更建议使用 API Key（个人订阅额度主要是为日常人工交互设计的，详见 [Anthropic](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance) 与 [OpenAI](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/auth) 的官方说明）。如果你用它对外提供服务，请使用 API Key。本项目为独立开源项目，与上述厂商无隶属或背书关系。 ## 更多文档 - [安装说明](INSTALL.md) - [规则与交付流水线配置手册](skills/agent-autoloop/SKILL.md) - [如何编写插件](docs/plugins.md) - [完整通信协议](docs/protocol.md) - [安全边界说明](SECURITY.md) - [参与贡献与交流](CONTRIBUTING.md) - [项目开发约定](AGENTS.md)
仓库目录 | 位置 | 放什么 | |---|---| | `kernel/` | 内核：决策、事实日志、状态投影、到期任务、规则匹配、接口行为与卡片表单 | | `host/` | 运行外壳：Node HTTP、文件与 SQLite 连接、时钟、配置、状态汇总、后台服务和插件加载 | | `protocol/` | 通信格式、JSON Schema、输入校验、HTTP 客户端和一致性检查 | | `worker/` | 接单程序：领活、运行 Agent、心跳与停止、读取和提交回执 | | `cli/`、`bin/` | 用户命令及启动入口，包括状态、回答、`why`、MCP、更新与卸载 | | `plugins/` | 内置 Agent、事件、通道和交付插件 | | `examples/recipes/` | 完整场景：规则、任务 Skill 和启用说明 | | `examples/plugins/`、`examples/skills/`、`examples/*.sh` | 最小插件模板、独立任务手册和 Shell 示例 | | `skills/agent-autoloop/` | 中台的正式配置与操作手册，安装时也提供给 Agent 使用 | | `docs/` | 通信协议、插件开发说明与中英文架构图 | | `tests/`、`sim/` | 日常行为测试，以及模拟、穷举、强杀和变异检查 | | `scripts/`、`.github/workflows/` | 性能与真机验证、安装冒烟脚本，以及 Windows / Linux / macOS CI | | 根目录文档与 `install.sh` | 中英文 README、安装说明、安全边界、开发约定、许可证与安装脚本 | 读代码可以从 `bin/agent-autoloop.ts` → `cli/main.ts` 开始，再按功能进入 `host/`、`worker/` 或 `plugins/`；内核设计先看[协议](docs/protocol.md)。同名文件分属不同层：`host/http.ts` 转换 Node 请求，`kernel/http.ts` 定义接口行为；`protocol/rules.ts` 校验输入，`kernel/rules.ts` 定义规则类型和匹配。

quick.headline: Anthropic explains how Claude agents remember things, and how "dreaming" fixes bad notes
quick.summary: Claude can review its old session logs offline, the way people replay memories during sleep, and correct notes it got wrong.
quick.why_it_matters: If you build agents that run across many sessions, saved notes can go stale or wrong, and this shows one way to catch that.

extra.source_text: Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward , but it must be lived forward . We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents. As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. The hippocampus plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only some experiences are consolidated into long-term knowledge. Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet rest , the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill those experiences and integrate them into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge. Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed sleep-time compute as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called dreaming (Figure 1). We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization. Claude can use dreaming to organize memory. This can correct mistakes, create notes, build new memory representations, or shape what’s preemptively loaded into future sessions. Memory notes By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), in-context learning (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and compaction (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window). In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can mark a memory as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called replay , helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory. Similarly, Claude can tag salient events in a session log as they happen, so they’re easier to find later, or it can write them to a memory store, such as a folder of memory notes (Figure 2). But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next? Claude can write notes to memory. Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions. Consider a task from Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0 , a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions. Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future. We ran the CL-Bench 1.0 task using Claude Managed Agents . Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a memory directory that persisted from one session to the next. Different models achieved different levels of success at creating their own learning loops. Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses. CL-Bench database task, comparing memory with a stateless baseline across models. Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed. Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong. Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3). Like Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both closed the loop, using memory to capture validated rules about how to best answer future questions. With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher. Claude has learned to judge salience We also evaluated Claude’s ability to play Pokémon Red , a game that challenges Claude to navigate complex long-horizon tasks, as a test of Claude’s judgment about what to save to memory. At the start of each run, we gave each model a folder of memory files that it could read from and write to while it played (Figure 4). We compared the memory folders from one run each of Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Fable 5, when each was about 10,000 steps into the game. A key difference we noticed was what each model thought was worth remembering. Sonnet 3.7 assumed everything might matter and wrote to memory indiscriminately. Its memory folder contained an archive of encounters, often with a separate file for each battle it fought, each item it found, and each non-player character it met. Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game). Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called global.md , and earned four badges. Claude’s memory directories for Sonnet 3.7 versus Fable 5 while playing Pokémon. Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date. As a result, as Claude progressed, it had to spend more time and resources combing through its memories rather than playing the game. Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself. Fable 5’s approach used memory for things the game didn’t explicitly tell it. Some of the kinds of information Sonnet 3.7 wrote to memory—such as how much money the player has or where the player is on the map—can be read off the screen every turn, so storing it is redundant. By contrast, memory files about strategy, plans, and tested rules exist only if Claude works them out, and they disappear unless Claude writes them down. Fable 5 organized its memory accordingly. Its global.md file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory. A locations folder held plans for navigating particular routes, and a gameplay folder held strategies based on what it had learned about how the game works. For example, after seven Poké Balls in a row failed to catch a Magikarp (one of the easiest Pokémon to catch), Claude wrote, “If 3+ balls fail in a row, VARY the timing (insert extra ‘wait’ presses between menu steps) - the catch landed right after doing this.” With a much smaller memory folder, Fable 5 progressed much further in the game than Sonnet 3.7. Opus 5.5 took a similar approach: it kept a small folder of memory notes that tracked its current goal and next steps, rewrote them as it played, and beat the game. Steering Claude to write memory We’ve found that it helps to tell Claude what memory is for, but not how to use it. On CL-Bench, we simply told Claude that a memory folder was available. That general guidance was enough for Opus 4.7 and Opus 5 to use memory effectively, and it gave both a noticeable boost in performance (Figure 3). We also tested giving the models specific rules about what they should write to memory, with one rule per test. We compared how much each model gained from memory with each rule against how much it gained without it. When we set a rule to “record only failures,” both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lost much of the performance boost that memory gave them (Figure 5, right). For stronger models, giving them freedom to judge salience was more effective than setting fixed rules in advance, and those rules could end up weakening performance. Left: Sonnet 4.6 on the CL-Bench database task with and without prompting to guide memory usage. Right: how much each model’s gain from memory changed when it was told to record only failures. We also noticed that steering helped older models the most. For instance, Sonnet 4.6 often didn’t read files from its memory directory and failed to test its theories about why an answer was wrong. In this case, prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering—and then to explicitly test its theories—nearly doubled its benchmark score (Figure 5, left). Sonnet 5 does this on its own. Without being prompted to, it read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times. By comparison, Sonnet 4.6 did this less than half of the time. With frontier Claude models, we typically give simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks them to or when something is clearly worth remembering, and we leave that judgment up to Claude. Dreaming can correct memory Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session. Dreaming gives Claude a way to test its notes against the original transcripts (Figure 6). We saw a positive example of this when Claude played Pokémon using Managed Agents with a mounted directory for its memories. Dreaming can correct mistakes in memory. In one part of the game, the player has to get through Mt. Moon, a cave system with its entrance on the west side of the map and its exit on the east. Near the entrance is a trap: a one-way ledge that drops the player onto the route they came from, with no clear way to climb back up. Claude was using the PokéCenter, a building at the mountain’s entrance, as a landmark, so whether it walked off the ledge depended on which side of the mountain it thought the PokéCenter was on. At one point, Claude wrote down (incorrectly) that the PokéCenter was on the east side. When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.” But Mt. Moon was not behind it. A few actions later, Claude went over the ledge and landed back on the route it had come from (Figure 7). Its navigation tool didn’t show the drop, so Claude concluded, “I overshot far west,” and that it had been on the correct side all along. It hadn’t. A corrected memory note changed the outcome in Pokémon. With the uncorrected note, Claude says, “Mt Moon is behind me,” heads for the next city, and ends up back on the route it came from. With the note corrected by dreaming, it says, “Now I need to find the Mt Moon cave entrance to re-enter,” and goes back into the cave. We then tested whether dreaming could help Claude avoid this trap. We ran dreaming
